stacks.name: Basics
stacks.description: What boosting is and why weak learners are the right ingredient.

cards.front: What problem does boosting solve, and what does it combine?
cards.back: It turns many weak learners (each slightly better than trivial) into one strong learner by adding them sequentially, each correcting the errors of those before it.

cards.front: One-line definition of a weak learner.
cards.back: Classification: error \(\le \tfrac12 - \gamma\) for a fixed edge \(\gamma>0\). Regression: optimally-scaled risk \(\le (1-\gamma)\mathrm{Var}(Y)\), i.e. correlated with the target above a fixed threshold.

cards.front: Why deliberately use weak (not strong) learners?
cards.back: Weak learners are high bias, low variance. Boosting drives down bias by combining many; strong learners would overfit fast and leave nothing for later rounds to correct.

cards.front: Why are decision stumps the canonical weak learner?
cards.back: They are low-capacity (one split), fast, and reliably beat the trivial baseline by a small margin without overfitting, exactly the weak-learner profile.
